content: The study by Bhatnagar (1996) evaluated children aged 3 to 24 months with diarrhea lasting at least 14 days but less than 12 weeks. These children, who had passed three or more liquid stools in the previous 24 hours, were recruited from diarrhea treatment units at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) and Kasturba Hospital in New Delhi, India, between February 1992 and January 1995. A total of 116 eligible children, including 23 girls, were randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group 1 (n=60) received a milk-based cereal diet, while Group 2 (n=56) received an egg-white-based cereal diet. Both diets were offered at 150 kcal/kg per day. However, the available records did not allow for data extraction for this review. The study was funded by the World Health Organization's Diarrheal Diseases Control Programme. The risk of bias was assessed as low for random sequence generation and allocation concealment, with stratified randomization and central allocation methods used. However, blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessment was unclear. The study by Brunser (1993) involved children from a low socioeconomic community in Santiago, Chile. Two consecutive cohorts of children were divided into two groups: one group received iron-fortified milk, and the other received control milk. Each cohort was followed for six months. Outcomes included the incidence of diarrhea, bowel movements, stool characteristics, and asymptomatic shedding of enteropathogens. The fortified milk contained 12 mg/L of iron, while the control milk contained 1 mg/L. The risk of bias was unclear for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and baseline characteristics, as these were not reported. The study by Chatchatee (2014) was a double-blind randomized controlled trial conducted in five countries (Malaysia, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, and Thailand). Healthy children aged 11 to 29 months attending daycare at least twice a week were randomly assigned to one of three groups. Group 1 received follow-on formula with added short-chain galacto-oligosaccharides, long-chain fructo-oligosaccharides, and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids. Group 2 received a control follow-on formula without these additions. Group 3, a non-randomized reference group, consumed cow’s milk. The study was funded by Danone Research. Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were judged to have a low risk of bias, but the lack of randomization in the reference group excluded it from meta-analysis. The study by Daly (1996) was a double-blind randomized cohort trial involving children aged 6 to 8 months living in Birmingham, UK. Children whose mothers had already transitioned them to unmodified cow’s milk were invited to participate. A total of 100 children were randomized into two groups: one group received fortified milk, while the other continued with cow’s milk. Developmental assessments were conducted at enrollment, 18 months, and 24 months. The study was funded by Farley Health Products. Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were judged to have a low risk of bias, with blinding of observers and researchers. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, and incomplete outcome data were minimal. The study by Ghisolfi (2012) was a non-randomized controlled study conducted in France. Children aged 12 to 24 months were divided into two groups based on their milk intake: one group consumed cow’s milk, and the other consumed follow-on formula. The study was funded by the French Association of Baby Food Industries. The risk of bias was high for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding, as these were not implemented. The study by Gill (1997) was a randomized controlled trial conducted in the UK and Ireland. Healthy term infants aged 6 months were randomly assigned to one of three groups: one group received iron-fortified follow-on formula, another received unfortified follow-on formula, and a reference group continued with cow’s milk. The study was funded by SMA Nutrition and Wyeth Laboratories. Random sequence generation was judged to have a low risk of bias, but allocation concealment and blinding were unclear. Baseline characteristics were well-balanced between randomized groups, but the reference group was not randomized. The study by Lovell (2018) was a double-blind randomized controlled trial conducted in Auckland, New Zealand, and Brisbane, Australia. Healthy 1-year-old children were randomly assigned to receive either a reduced-protein follow-on formula or unfortified cow’s milk. Dietary intakes were collected at baseline and at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months post-randomization. The primary outcome was body composition, with secondary outcomes including micronutrient status and cognitive development. The study was funded by Danone Nutricia Research. Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were judged to have a low risk of bias, with blinding of researchers and participants. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, and incomplete outcome data were minimal.
